name: FlorisBoard — Snygg theme engine
source_of_truth: Primary source code reading of github.com/florisboard/florisboard (main branch), module :lib:snygg and app/.../ime/theme, plus docs.florisboard.org
rendering_approach: Genuine per-key, selector-based *styling* — not per-key bitmaps and not a single background paste. Every UI element (including each key) is a Compose composable that queries the compiled theme at draw time for its own resolved property set, so each key can legitimately differ from its neighbours. Concretely: `SnyggTheme.query(elementName, attributes, selector, parentStyle)` returns a resolved `SnyggPropertySet`, and the Snygg Compose wrappers (`SnyggBox`, `SnyggButton`, `SnyggRow`, `SnyggColumn`, `SnyggText`, `SnyggIcon`, `SnyggIconButton`, `SnyggChip`, `SnyggListItem`, `SnyggSpacer` in `lib/snygg/.../ui/`) translate that property set into a Compose modifier chain. There is no per-key drawable asset: a key's visual is composed from vector-ish primitives — `background` (solid color), `shape` (rounded-corner/cut-corner), `border-color`/`border-width`, `shadow-elevation`/`shadow-color`, `padding`/`margin`, plus text properties for the label. A raster `background-image` exists but is scoped to container elements (the `window` rule) rather than to individual key caps, so the model is best described as: **per-element vector/property drawing, with an optional whole-window image behind a transparent-or-translucent key layer**. That makes it a hybrid only at the window level; at the key level it is pure per-key property drawing.
selector_and_state_model:
This is the strongest part of Snygg and the reason it is the clearest per-key selector example available. A rule is `<element>[<attr>=<values>]:<selector>`.

(1) ELEMENT NAME — matches `[a-zA-Z0-9-]+`, drawn from a fixed vocabulary declared in `app/.../ime/theme/FlorisImeUi.kt`. Roughly 90 element names exist, e.g. `root`, `window`, `window-inner`, `window-move-handle`, `window-resize-handle`, `key`, `key-hint`, `key-popup-box`, `key-popup-element`, `key-popup-extended-indicator`, `smartbar`, `smartbar-shared-actions-row`, `smartbar-shared-actions-toggle`, `smartbar-extended-actions-row`, `smartbar-action-key`, `smartbar-action-tile`, `smartbar-action-tile-icon`, `smartbar-action-tile-text`, `smartbar-candidates-row`, `smartbar-candidate-word`, `smartbar-candidate-word-text`, `smartbar-candidate-word-secondary-text`, `smartbar-candidate-clip`, `smartbar-candidate-spacer`, `smartbar-actions-editor`, `media`, `media-emoji-key`, `media-emoji-subheader`, `media-emoji-tab`, `media-emoji-key-popup-box`, `media-bottom-row`, `media-bottom-row-button`, `clipboard-header`, `clipboard-item`, `clipboard-item-popup`, `clipboard-item-timestamp`, `clipboard-filter-chip`, `clipboard-grid`, `clipboard-clear-all-dialog`, `one-handed-panel`, `one-handed-panel-button`, `subtype-panel`, `subtype-panel-list-item`, `glide-trail`, `incognito-mode-indicator`, `inline-autofill-chip`, `extracted-landscape-input-field`, and the many clipboard/smartbar sub-elements.

(2) ATTRIBUTES — bracket notation `[key=value1,value2]`. The declared attribute keys (`FlorisImeUi.Attr`) are `code`, `mode`, `shiftstate`, and `windowmode`. Values may be integers, **integer ranges** (`0..10`), or backtick-quoted strings (`` `value` ``). `code` is the key code, which is exactly the "target one specific key" capability: e.g. targeting Enter. `shiftstate` gives shift/caps/caps-lock differentiation; `mode` and `windowmode` give layout/context differentiation (e.g. floating vs fixed window). `SnyggAttributes` exposes `including()`, `excluding()`, `toggling()` to derive modified copies.

(3) SELECTOR (pseudo-class) — the `SnyggSelector` enum in `SnyggRule.kt` declares exactly five values, serialized with a colon prefix: `PRESSED("pressed")`, `FOCUS("focus")`, `HOVER("hover")`, `DISABLED("disabled")`, and `NONE("none")` (serialized as empty string). So the state vocabulary is `:pressed`, `:focus`, `:hover`, `:disabled`, plus the unselected base rule.

Concrete Kotlin-DSL examples from `FlorisImeThemeBaseStyle.kt`:
```kotlin
FlorisImeUi.Key.elementName {
    background = `var`("--surface")
    foreground = `var`("--on-surface")
    fontSize = fontSize(22.sp)
    shadowElevation = size(2.dp)
    shape = `var`("--shape")
    textMaxLines = textMaxLines(1)
}
FlorisImeUi.Key.elementName(selector = SnyggSelector.PRESSED) {
    background = `var`("--surface-variant")
}
FlorisImeUi.Key.elementName(FlorisImeUi.Attr.Code to listOf(KeyCode.ENTER)) {
    background = `var`("--primary")
}
FlorisImeUi.SmartbarActionKey.elementName(selector = SnyggSelector.DISABLED) {
    foreground = `var`("--on-background-disabled")
}
```
The JSON stylesheet form uses the same string keys, e.g. `"key"`, `"key:pressed"`, `"key[code=13]"`.

SPECIFICITY / CASCADE — this is *not* CSS weight arithmetic. `SnyggRule` is a sealed interface implementing `compareTo()`, and the documented total ordering is: `@defines` first, then `@font` (multiple fonts sorted by fontName), then element rules sorted first by element name, then by attributes/selectors. `SnyggTheme.compileFrom()` groups rules by element name and calls `rulesets.sortBy { it.first }`. At query time it iterates the sorted list and applies **every** matching rule in order — later matches overwrite earlier ones (`if (rule.isMatchForQuery(attributes, selector)) editor.applyAll(propertySet, parentStyle, fontSizeMultiplier)`). So precedence is deterministic sort-order-based last-writer-wins, not a computed specificity score. Matching requires ALL declared attributes to be satisfied (`if (!attrValues.contains(queryValue)) return false`) and the selector to match exactly or be `NONE` (`return this == SnyggSelector.NONE || this == query`), meaning a base rule also applies under `:pressed` and the `:pressed` rule then layers on top. That is the inherit-and-override cascade.

INHERITANCE — two-level. (a) The `root` rule is a meta-rule whose properties are inherited by everything, implicitly or explicitly depending on the property. (b) Parent-to-child inheritance via `editor.inheritImplicitly(parentStyle)`. Each property declares an `InheritBehavior` of `IMPLICITLY_OR_EXPLICITLY` or `EXPLICITLY_ONLY` (enum in `SnyggSpecDecl.kt`). Text-ish properties (`foreground`, `font-family`, `font-size`, `font-style`, `font-weight`, `letter-spacing`, `line-height`, `text-align`, `text-decoration-line`, `text-max-lines`, `text-overflow`) inherit implicitly; box-ish properties (`background`, `border-*`, `shadow-*`, `shape`, `padding`, `margin`, `clip`, `background-image`, `content-scale`) do not.

VARIABLES — `@defines` block holds variables named `--[a-zA-Z0-9-]+`, referenced as `` `var`("--name") `` in DSL / `var(--name)` in JSON. Substitution happens at **compile** time, not query time: `if (value is SnyggDefinedVarValue) { editor.properties[property] = variables[value.key] ?: SnyggUndefinedValue }`.
rendering_pipeline:
Jetpack Compose, running inside an `InputMethodService`. FlorisBoard is one of the few shipping IMEs that solved the well-known Compose-in-IME blocker (a `ComposeView` inside an IME's `onCreateInputView()` throws because the view tree has no `ViewTreeLifecycleOwner`/`SavedStateRegistryOwner`); it does this by having the service itself implement `LifecycleOwner` and `SavedStateRegistryOwner` and attaching them to the input view's tree. Snygg's Compose layer is `lib/snygg/.../ui/` (`SnyggBox`, `SnyggButton`, `SnyggRow`, `SnyggColumn`, `SnyggText`, `SnyggIcon`, `SnyggIconButton`, `SnyggChip`, `SnyggListItem`, `SnyggSpacer`, plus `SnyggUi.kt` with modifier extensions `snyggBackground()`, `snyggBorder()`, `snyggShadow()`, `snyggPadding()`, `snyggMargin()`).

Per-keystroke cost is mitigated by making theme lookup cheap and memoized rather than by avoiding recomposition: the stylesheet is compiled **once** into a `SnyggTheme` (variables already substituted, fonts already resolved to `FontFamily` objects, rules already grouped by element name and pre-sorted), so a key press does a small filtered iteration over one element's ruleset rather than re-parsing anything. Style queries are wrapped in `remember()` keyed on element name, attributes, and color schemes; custom font families are `remember(snyggTheme)`-ed and resolved with `runBlocking` once at theme-apply time. A pressed-state change therefore recomposes only the affected key subtree.

Caveat: no explicit query-result cache is visible inside `SnyggTheme.query` itself — the memoization lives at the Compose `remember` layer. Also worth noting `snyggMargin()` is implemented with Compose `padding()` (Compose has no true outer margin), so margin and padding differ by where they sit in the modifier chain rather than by mechanism.
compositing_scrim_model:
Layer stack, outermost to innermost, is expressed as a Compose modifier chain rather than a documented "scrim" feature:

1. `window` element paints the keyboard backdrop: `background` (solid color) and optionally `background-image` (a `flex://` URI to a bundled raster) governed by `content-scale`.
2. `window-inner` and the smartbar/key grid sit above it.
3. Each `key` paints, in modifier order: `snyggShadow()` → `shadow(elevation, shape, clip = false, colors)`; then `snyggBackground()` → `background(color, shape)`, which also applies `clip` when `allowClip && style.clip !is SnyggNoValue`; then `snyggBorder()` → `border(width, color, shape)`; then `snyggPadding()`. Note shadow is drawn with `clip = false` so the elevation shadow is not cut by the key's own shape.
4. Key label/icon on top via `SnyggText`/`SnyggIcon` using the inherited `foreground`.

CRITICAL FINDING — **there is no dedicated scrim, dim, brightness, or blur property in Snygg.** Reading `Snygg.kt`, the complete property vocabulary has no `opacity`, no `blur`, no `overlay`, no `dim`. Likewise `SnyggAppearanceValue.kt` implements only `SnyggStaticColorValue` (`rgba(r,g,b,a)`, `rgb(r,g,b)`, `transparent`, `#RRGGBB`, `#RRGGBBAA`), `SnyggDynamicLightColorValue` (`dynamic-light-color(colorName)`), and `SnyggDynamicDarkColorValue` (`dynamic-dark-color(colorName)`) — **`LinearGradient` and `RadialGradient` exist only as commented-out declarations and are not implemented.** So there is no gradient support either.

The practical consequence: legibility over a background image is achieved entirely by the theme author choosing a semi-transparent key `background` via the alpha channel of `rgba()`/`#RRGGBBAA`, and/or a semi-transparent solid `background` on `window` composited over the `background-image`. There is no engine-provided scrim with a default opacity value, so no default scrim opacity exists to quote. This is a meaningful gap versus commercial theme keyboards (Facemoji/Gboard) which ship an explicit brightness/opacity slider.
asset_types: Very asset-light by design — the engine is properties-first, not bitmap-first. Key caps carry **no** image assets at all: no 9-patch PNGs, no per-key drawables, no per-state bitmaps. Shapes come from `shape` values (rounded-corner and cut-corner, sized in dp or as a percentage, e.g. `roundedCornerShape(8.dp)` or `roundedCornerShape(20)`). The only raster assets in a theme are (a) a `background-image` for the `window` rule and (b) custom font files. Both are added as extension assets and referenced by a `flex://` URI (`SnyggUriValue`). Fonts come in two flavors: five built-in generic families assignable via `font-family`, and custom fonts declared with an `@font` annotation rule carrying `src` plus optional `font-style`/`font-weight` — i.e. multiple font source sets per family, CSS `@font-face`-style. Because there are no per-density drawables, Android density bucketing (mdpi/hdpi/xhdpi/…) is essentially irrelevant to a Snygg theme; everything is dp/sp-based and resolution-independent. Documented image formats and size limits are thin — the docs page on assets does not state supported formats or ceilings. [uncertain]
theme_package_manifest_format:
A theme ships as a `.flex` file — a ZIP archive with an `extension.json` manifest at the archive root. Skeleton:
```json
{
  "$": "ime.extension.theme",
  "meta": {
    "id": "<extension_id>",
    "version": "<version_string>",
    "title": "...",
    "description": "...",
    "keywords": [...],
    "maintainers": [...],
    "license": "<FSF_or_OSI_identifier>"
  },
  "themes": [
    {
      "id": "<theme_id>",
      "label": "...",
      "authors": [...],
      "isNight": false,
      "materialYouFlags": { "paletteStyle": "...", "contrastLevel": ..., "specVersion": ... },
      "stylesheetPath": "stylesheets/<theme_id>.json"
    }
  ]
}
```
The `$` field is a polymorphic type discriminator (`ime.extension.theme`) — the same manifest shape is reused for language-pack and keyboard extensions. Folder layout inside the ZIP: `extension.json` at root, stylesheets under `stylesheets/<theme_id>.json` (auto-loaded from that conventional path), and imported fonts/images as sibling asset files referenced by `flex://` URIs. One `.flex` may carry multiple themes (the `themes` array), which is how a pack ships a day + night pair.

Stylesheets themselves are authored either as JSON (`{ "@defines": {...}, "key": {...}, "key:pressed": {...} }`) or as the Kotlin DSL (`SnyggStylesheet.v2 { ... }`) used for the built-in base style. There is a `SnyggJsonSchemaGenerator.kt` in the snygg module that emits a JSON Schema for the stylesheet format, which is how editor tooling gets validation. Notably, only theme extensions can currently be created dynamically in-app; language-pack and keyboard extensions are only partially functional. No signing scheme is documented for `.flex`. [uncertain: whether stylesheetPath is an explicit manifest field or purely convention]
token_count_tiering:
**24 style properties**, enumerated exhaustively in `Snygg.kt` (Snygg v2): `background`, `background-image`, `content-scale`, `border-color`, `border-style` (declared but unsupported), `border-width`, `clip`, `font-family`, `font-size`, `font-style`, `font-weight`, `foreground`, `letter-spacing`, `line-height`, `margin`, `padding`, `shadow-color`, `shadow-elevation`, `shape`, `src`, `text-align`, `text-decoration-line`, `text-max-lines`, `text-overflow`. Plus two annotation rules: `@defines` and `@font`.

The combinatorial surface is much larger than 24, because those 24 properties are applied across ~90 element names × 4 attribute keys (`code`, `mode`, `shiftstate`, `windowmode`) × 5 selector states. A maximal theme is therefore a large document; a minimal one can be a handful of `@defines` variables plus overrides on `window` and `key`.

There is **no formal simple-vs-advanced tier** in the format itself. The tiering is provided by tooling and convention instead: (a) the recommended authoring workflow is to fork an existing stylesheet rather than start empty, so authors edit a small delta; (b) the `@defines` variable block acts as the de-facto "simple tier" — retheming by editing ~8 variables (`--primary`, `--primary-variant`, `--secondary`, `--background`, `--surface`, `--on-primary`, `--on-surface`, `--shape` in the base style) cascades everywhere, while touching individual element rules is the "advanced tier". Value types are backed by dedicated encoders: `SnyggAppearanceValue`, `SnyggFontValue`, `SnyggPaddingValue`, `SnyggShapeValue`, `SnyggSizeValue`, `SnyggTextValue`, `SnyggUriValue`, `SnyggVarValue`.
theme_versioning_forward_compat: Versioning is explicit and the compatibility story is blunt. The stylesheet format carries an engine version — the DSL entry point is literally `SnyggStylesheet.v2 { ... }` — and the manifest carries `meta.version` for the extension itself. Snygg v1 (FlorisBoard ≤0.4) and Snygg v2 (≥0.5) are **hard-incompatible with no automatic upgrade path**; the docs state v0.4 themes simply do not work on v0.5. Within a version, forward compat is lenient rather than strict: unresolvable variable references degrade to `SnyggUndefinedValue` (`variables[value.key] ?: SnyggUndefinedValue`) instead of failing the load, missing properties fall back through the inherit cascade to `root` and ultimately to the built-in `FlorisImeThemeBaseStyle`, and a property the running build doesn't know is ignored. So adding new tokens over time does NOT break older theme files — an old theme just renders without the new tokens. The reverse (a new theme on an old build) also degrades rather than crashes. The breaking risk is concentrated at major engine-version boundaries and at element-name renames, since element names are the join key between stylesheet and code. [uncertain: exact behavior on an unrecognized element name — likely silently unused]
color_extraction_dynamic_tinting: Both models are supported, and they coexist in one stylesheet. Pre-baked: `SnyggStaticColorValue` accepts `rgba(r, g, b, a)`, `rgb(r, g, b)`, `transparent`, `#RRGGBB`, and `#RRGGBBAA`. Dynamic: `SnyggDynamicLightColorValue` and `SnyggDynamicDarkColorValue`, written as `dynamic-light-color(<colorName>)` / `dynamic-dark-color(<colorName>)`, where `<colorName>` names a Material 3 color role. These resolve against the Android 12+ Material You palette extracted from the system wallpaper. Resolution is deliberately **late** — after rule matching, during query, dynamic colors are converted using the active light/dark scheme — so the same compiled theme serves both schemes without recompilation. The manifest's per-theme `materialYouFlags` (paletteStyle, contrastLevel, specVersion) tunes how the dynamic palette is generated. `WallpaperChangeReceiver.kt` in the theme package listens for wallpaper changes so the palette refreshes. Notably this is **wallpaper-derived, not background-image-derived**: there is no Palette-API extraction from the theme's own `background-image`, and no per-app color adaptation à la Chrooma. Theme variants are day / night / pure-night (OLED) / borderless, with `isNight` in the manifest and `ThemeMode.kt` driving selection.
contrast_enforcement_accessibility:
**No automatic contrast validation.** This is a real finding, not an information gap: the complete 24-property vocabulary in `Snygg.kt` contains no contrast, minimum-contrast, or auto-foreground property, and `SnyggTheme.query` performs no WCAG/APCA check between the resolved `foreground` and the composited `background`. Legibility is left entirely to the theme author. The engine cannot in general do the check anyway, because the true composited backdrop under a key may include a `window` `background-image` that Snygg never samples.

What exists instead are author-facing escape hatches rather than enforcement:
- `border-color` + `border-width` on `key` give a key-outline escape hatch, and "borderless" vs bordered is a first-class theme variant concept in FlorisBoard.
- A dedicated `pure night (OLED)` variant, and the day/night split via `isNight`, ensure a legible option exists per ambient mode.
- `materialYouFlags.contrastLevel` in the manifest is the one contrast-aware knob, but it tunes Material You palette generation (which does guarantee role-pair contrast within the M3 spec), not the theme's own hand-picked colors.
- `foreground` inherits implicitly from `root`, so a single legible text color can be enforced globally by the author in one place.
- `shadow-color`/`shadow-elevation` can be used to lift a key off a busy background.

So: automatic for dynamic-color themes (inherited from Material You's own contrast guarantees plus `contrastLevel`), fully manual for hand-authored static themes. There is no high-contrast override that a *user* can force on top of a third-party theme. [uncertain: whether any accessibility-service-driven high-contrast override exists elsewhere in the app outside the Snygg module]
background_geometry_adaptation:
Handled through the `content-scale` property and through the element vocabulary rather than through per-geometry art. `background-image` is set on the `window` rule and paired with `content-scale`, which maps to Compose's `ContentScale` (Crop / Fit / FillBounds / Inside etc.), so one image survives variable keyboard height and portrait↔landscape by crop-or-fit rather than by shipping multiple images. This is materially better than the marketplace-keyboard norm of shipping separate portrait and landscape wallpapers.

Geometry variants are addressable as first-class theming targets, which is unusual:
- Floating/fixed windowing has its own attribute key `windowmode`, so a rule can differ between floating and docked — e.g. `window[windowmode=floating]` can use a different image or scale.
- Floating-mode chrome has dedicated elements: `window-move-handle`, `window-resize-handle`, `window-resize-action`, `window-resize-overlay-fixed`, `floating-dock-to-fixed-indicator`.
- One-handed mode has `one-handed-panel` and `one-handed-panel-button`.
- Landscape-extracted (fullscreen) input mode has `extracted-landscape-input-layout`, `extracted-landscape-input-field`, `extracted-landscape-input-action`.
- `window` vs `window-inner` separates the outer surface (which the image sits on) from the inner content area, so insets/one-handed offsets don't distort the art.

Because key visuals are properties (shape/border/color) and not sliced bitmaps, keys themselves rescale cleanly at any height — nothing stretches or pixelates. Tablet handling is not separately documented. [uncertain: tablet-specific behavior, and whether `content-scale` defaults to Crop]
layout_locale_independence:
Strong — this falls out of the architecture rather than being a specific feature. Because there is no whole-keyboard key-grid bitmap and no per-key art keyed to a grid position, changing key count or layout cannot break theme art. Rules bind to *semantic* element names and key codes, not to coordinates or indices, so a theme authored on QWERTY renders correctly on AZERTY, QWERTZ, Dvorak, or any non-Latin layout without modification. Turning the number row on or off just adds/removes `key` instances that all match the same `key` rule. RTL is a Compose layout-direction concern that the theme is agnostic to, since `padding`/`margin` resolve through Compose's direction-aware layout.

The one genuine coupling is `code`-attribute rules: a rule like `key[code=<X>]` only fires where that key code exists, so a theme that specially styles a key absent from some layout silently loses that accent on those layouts. This degrades gracefully (the base `key` rule still applies) rather than breaking. Range syntax (`0..10`) helps here — an author can style whole code ranges instead of enumerating layout-specific codes. Split layout is covered by the same reasoning plus the `mode`/`windowmode` attributes. [uncertain: whether a distinct split-layout element or attribute value exists]
non_key_surface_coverage:
Exceptionally broad — this is arguably Snygg's second-biggest advantage after selectors. Roughly 90 themeable element names cover essentially every surface, not just key caps:
- **Suggestion/candidate strip**: `smartbar`, `smartbar-candidates-row`, `smartbar-candidate-word`, `smartbar-candidate-word-text`, `smartbar-candidate-word-secondary-text`, `smartbar-candidate-clip`, `smartbar-candidate-clip-icon`, `smartbar-candidate-clip-text`, `smartbar-candidate-spacer`.
- **Toolbar / action row**: `smartbar-shared-actions-row`, `smartbar-shared-actions-toggle`, `smartbar-extended-actions-row`, `smartbar-extended-actions-toggle`, `smartbar-action-key`, `smartbar-action-tile` (+ `-icon`, `-text`), `smartbar-actions-overflow`, `smartbar-actions-overflow-customize-button`, and the whole editor: `smartbar-actions-editor`, `-header`, `-header-button`, `-subheader`, `-tile-grid`, `-tile`.
- **Emoji / media panel**: `media`, `media-emoji-key`, `media-emoji-subheader`, `media-emoji-tab`, `media-bottom-row`, `media-bottom-row-button`.
- **Key-preview popup and long-press mini-keyboard**: `key-popup-box`, `key-popup-element`, `key-popup-extended-indicator`, and emoji equivalents `media-emoji-key-popup-box`, `media-emoji-key-popup-element`, `media-emoji-key-popup-extended-indicator`. Plus `key-hint` for the hint glyph.
- **Clipboard sheet**: ~28 elements — `clipboard-header`(+button/text), `clipboard-subheader`, `clipboard-content`, `clipboard-filter-row`, `clipboard-filter-chip`(+icon/text), `clipboard-grid`, `clipboard-item`(+description/timestamp/popup), `clipboard-item-actions`/`-action`/`-action-icon`/`-action-text`, `clipboard-clear-all-dialog`(+message/buttons/button), `clipboard-history-disabled-title`/`-message`/`-button`, `clipboard-history-locked-title`/`-message`.
- **Other**: `subtype-panel` (+header/list/list-item/list-item-icon-leading/list-item-text), `one-handed-panel`(+button), `glide-trail` (the swipe-typing trail is themeable), `incognito-mode-indicator`, `inline-autofill-chip`, `extracted-landscape-input-*`, `window-move-handle`/`-resize-handle`/`-resize-action`.

System nav bar color is not a Snygg element and appears to be handled outside the theme engine, unlike Chrooma which explicitly themes it. [uncertain: nav-bar handling]
sound_haptic_theming: **Not part of the theme engine.** Key sounds and haptics are user preferences in FlorisBoard's settings (volume/strength toggles), not properties a `.flex` theme can carry — the 24-property Snygg vocabulary has no audio or haptic property, and no element carries a sound reference. This is a deliberate scope boundary: Snygg themes visual surfaces only. Consequence for a theme marketplace: a FlorisBoard theme cannot ship a custom key-press sound the way Facemoji themes can, so sound is not a differentiator a theme author can sell. Underlying platform APIs would be `AudioManager`/`SoundPool` for sound and `HapticFeedbackConstants`/`Vibrator`/`VibratorManager` for haptics, driven by the IME rather than the theme. [uncertain: exact APIs, since this sits outside the module examined]
platform_apis_frameworks: Android-only. Kotlin + Jetpack Compose for all rendering, hosted in an `InputMethodService` that implements `LifecycleOwner` and `SavedStateRegistryOwner` to make Compose viable inside an IME. Compose primitives used by Snygg's modifier layer: `Modifier.background(color, shape)`, `Modifier.border(width, color, shape)`, `Modifier.shadow(elevation, shape, clip = false, colors)`, `Modifier.padding(values)`, `Modifier.clip(...)`, `ContentScale` for images, `FontFamily` + `Font` for typography, `TextAlign`/`TextOverflow`/`maxLines` for text. Material 3 / Material You dynamic color (Android 12+, API 31+) supplies `dynamic-light-color()`/`dynamic-dark-color()`, with a `WallpaperChangeReceiver` (a `BroadcastReceiver`) to invalidate on wallpaper change. `kotlinx.serialization` handles the JSON stylesheet and `extension.json`. Gradle multi-module layout with `:lib:snygg` as a deliberately standalone, app-agnostic module — Snygg has no FlorisBoard-specific knowledge; the IME-specific vocabulary lives in `app/.../ime/theme/FlorisImeUi.kt`, which is a clean seam worth copying. Written in Kotlin DSL Gradle (`build.gradle.kts`).
delivery_installation_pipeline:
Three routes, all converging on the same on-disk shape:
1. **Bundled** — `FlorisImeThemeBaseStyle.kt` is a compiled-in Kotlin DSL stylesheet that ships in the APK and acts as the always-present fallback/base. Default day/night/OLED/borderless themes ship this way.
2. **Downloaded `.flex`** — from the official FlorisBoard Addons store or any third-party source. Flow is: download → open the file → choose FlorisBoard → import → select stylesheet. Extensions are keyed by `meta.id`; re-importing the same id **overwrites** the existing version, which is also the update mechanism. The Addons & Extensions settings screen offers an update search.
3. **Created in-app** — Themes → Theme extensions → Create extension, seeded from an existing stylesheet.

On disk, an imported `.flex` is unzipped into a per-theme directory. `FlorisAssetResolver` receives a `ThemeInfo` carrying a `loadedDir` property that is the base path for all asset lookups; stylesheet `flex://` URIs resolve relative to that directory. So assets land in app-private internal storage under a per-extension folder, not in shared storage. Nothing is installed as a separate Android package — there is **no legacy plugin-APK model** here, which is a clean contrast with the commercial theme keyboards that historically shipped each theme as its own installable APK. No signing or store-side verification of `.flex` files is documented, and third-party sources are explicitly supported with the same import flow as the official store.
permission_store_policy_surface:
Low-friction relative to commercial keyboards. Android has no equivalent of iOS Full Access — an IME is enabled in system settings and then simply runs; theming needs no additional runtime permission. Importing a `.flex` goes through the system file picker / `ACTION_VIEW` intent, so no broad storage permission is required. Material You dynamic color needs no permission, though wallpaper-change observation uses a `BroadcastReceiver`.

Policy posture: FlorisBoard is GPLv3 and distributed via F-Droid and Google Play. Because themes are inert declarative data (JSON + images + fonts) and contain no executable code, downloadable themes do not run afoul of Play's restriction on downloading executable code at runtime — a genuinely important design property for any theme marketplace. The manifest even carries a `license` field expecting an FSF/OSI identifier, reflecting the project's licensing hygiene for shared themes. A keyboard is a sensitive app category on Play (it can observe all typed input), so the app faces data-safety-disclosure scrutiny generally, but the theming subsystem specifically adds no permission surface. [uncertain: whether the Addons store applies any submission review]
memory_performance_budget:
No numeric memory ceiling is documented, and none is enforced by the engine — but Android IMEs face nothing like the iOS keyboard extension's hard ~30-40MB dirty / ~77MB total limit, so the pressure is structurally lower. What FlorisBoard does instead is keep the theme representation intrinsically cheap:
- **No bitmaps in the hot path.** Key caps are colors, shapes, borders and shadows. A theme with no `background-image` decodes zero images, so per-key art contributes ~0 to the heap. This is the single biggest budget decision in the design and the main reason Snygg-style theming is cheaper than the 9-patch-per-key marketplace model.
- **Compile once, query many.** `SnyggTheme.compileFrom()` does variable substitution, font resolution and rule sorting up front; the runtime path is a filtered iteration over one element's pre-sorted ruleset. Per-keystroke cost is a small map/list walk, not parsing.
- **Memoization at the Compose boundary.** Style queries are `remember()`-ed on (element, attributes, color schemes); font families are `remember(snyggTheme)`-ed and resolved once via `runBlocking`.
- Only `background-image` introduces real bitmap cost, and it is one image for the whole window rather than N images for N keys.

No max decoded bitmap size, downsampling policy, bitmap cache, or eviction strategy is documented in the theming code examined — plausibly delegated to whatever image loader paints the `background-image`, but this is not visible in `SnyggUi.kt` (which contains no Painter/ContentScale image path), suggesting the image is painted elsewhere. This is the weakest-documented area of an otherwise well-specified engine, and a real risk for large user-supplied backgrounds. [uncertain: all bitmap-budget specifics; no documented ceiling, downsampling, or cache policy found]
untrusted_theme_validation_security:
Better than expected for a hobby-scale project, and the one concrete hardening measure is worth copying. `FlorisAssetResolver` defends against path traversal / zip-slip-style escapes when resolving `flex://` URIs: it (a) validates the URI uses the `flex://` scheme with no authority component, (b) canonicalizes the resolved path to absolute form, (c) verifies the canonical path **starts with** the theme's base directory (`loadedDir`) — the code path logs "Calculated path does not start with base path" on violation — and (d) confirms the target exists and is a regular file, not a directory. Failures log via `flogError` with the offending URI and theme info, and resolve to nothing rather than throwing.

Malformed manifests/stylesheets are handled by `kotlinx.serialization` decoding, and the engine degrades rather than crashes on semantic problems: unknown variable references become `SnyggUndefinedValue`, missing properties fall back through the inherit chain to `FlorisImeThemeBaseStyle`. A JSON Schema is machine-generated by `SnyggJsonSchemaGenerator.kt`, giving editors/tooling a validation contract.

Not found: any image decode-size limit (a decompression-bomb PNG remains a plausible DoS), any `.flex` signature verification, any archive entry-count/uncompressed-size cap at unzip time, and any sandboxing of custom font files (font parsers are a classic native-code attack surface). Themes contain no executable code, which bounds the worst case considerably. [uncertain: unzip-time protections and decode limits]
open_source_reference_availability: Fully open source and the single best reference available for per-key selector-based theming. License GPLv3. Repo: https://github.com/florisboard/florisboard. The theme engine is deliberately factored as a standalone, app-agnostic Gradle module — **`lib/snygg/src/main/kotlin/org/florisboard/lib/snygg/`** — containing `Snygg.kt` (property vocabulary), `SnyggRule.kt` (selector/attribute parsing, `SnyggSelector` enum, rule ordering), `SnyggTheme.kt` (compile + query), `SnyggStylesheet.kt` / `SnyggStylesheetEditor.kt`, `SnyggPropertySet.kt` / `SnyggPropertySetEditor.kt`, `SnyggSpecDecl.kt` (spec-declaration DSL + `InheritBehavior`), `SnyggJsonSchemaGenerator.kt`, plus `value/` (12 value-encoder files) and `ui/` (11 Compose wrapper files). The IME-specific element vocabulary is separate, in **`app/src/main/kotlin/dev/patrickgold/florisboard/ime/theme/`** — `FlorisImeUi.kt` (element names + attribute keys), `FlorisImeThemeBaseStyle.kt` (the default stylesheet, a readable end-to-end DSL example), `ThemeManager.kt`, `ThemeExtension.kt`, `FlorisAssetResolver.kt`, `ThemeMode.kt`, `WallpaperChangeReceiver.kt`. Docs at https://docs.florisboard.org/themes/ (thin on syntax — the source is more informative). DeepWiki index at https://deepwiki.com/florisboard/florisboard. Design discussion in GitHub Discussion #1531 and Issue #256 (background images).
authoring_tooling_preview_generation: A full in-app visual theme editor ships with the app — no external toolchain needed, which is a notable strength. Path: Themes → Manage theme extensions → select theme → Edit on a stylesheet. The editor has three sections: (1) **Stylesheet metadata**, backed by `extension.json`; (2) **`@defines`**, where variables matching `--[a-zA-Z0-9-]+` are declared, each holding one Snygg property value; (3) **Rules**, where element rules and their properties are edited. An asset manager handles importing fonts and images into the extension archive, with rename and delete by tapping a filename. Setting a background is a concrete editor flow: add `background-image` to the `window` rule, choose "Uri reference" as the value type, then pick the file via a file finder. Values are typed in the UI — a value can be a reference to another value (variable), a solid color, a switch, or raw text. Creation is fork-first: "Create extension" then choose an existing stylesheet as a base rather than starting empty. `SnyggJsonSchemaGenerator.kt` emits a JSON Schema, enabling external editors to validate hand-written stylesheets. **No store-thumbnail/preview-variant generation requirement exists** — unlike marketplace keyboards that demand multiple rendered preview images per theme, FlorisBoard's Addons listing has no documented multi-variant preview spec. Live-preview fidelity while editing is not explicitly documented. [uncertain: live preview behavior and Addons listing image requirements]
cross_platform_token_parity: Not applicable in practice — FlorisBoard is **Android-only**; there is no iOS build, so no theme definition is shared across platforms and no parity has been attempted. That said, the format is unusually portable in principle, and this is the interesting part for a cross-platform product: the stylesheet is platform-neutral declarative JSON, and Snygg is intentionally split into an app-agnostic `:lib:snygg` module plus an IME-specific element vocabulary, so the *format* could be reimplemented on another platform by writing a new renderer against the same 24 properties. Most properties map cleanly onto SwiftUI equivalents (`background`→`.background`, `shape`→`.clipShape(RoundedRectangle)`, `border-*`→`.overlay(stroke)`, `padding`/`margin`→`.padding`, `font-*`/`text-*`→SwiftUI text modifiers, `content-scale`→`.aspectRatio`/`.scaledToFill`). The genuinely platform-bound tokens are `dynamic-light-color()`/`dynamic-dark-color()` and the `materialYouFlags` block, which depend on Android 12+ wallpaper-derived Material You and have no iOS equivalent; `shadow-elevation` is also Android-elevation-flavored rather than iOS's offset/radius shadow model. Implementation is entirely Kotlin/Compose and thus not reusable as code.
animation_budget: **No animation support in the theme engine — a firm negative finding, not a documentation gap.** The complete 24-property vocabulary in `Snygg.kt` contains no animation, transition, duration, or frame-rate property. `background-image` is a static raster referenced by URI; there is no Lottie, GIF, APNG, or video value type. `SnyggAppearanceValue.kt` implements only static and dynamic colors, with `LinearGradient` and `RadialGradient` present merely as commented-out declarations — so even animated gradients are unavailable. Consequently there is no frame-rate cap to document and no idle-pause policy, because nothing animates from the theme's side. GitHub Issue #256 ("Add image or animation as keyboard background", opened Jan 2021, labeled accepted proposal) requested animated backgrounds explicitly; the static-image half shipped in v0.5 / Snygg v2, the animation half did not. Any motion visible in the keyboard (ripples, glide trail — `glide-trail` is a themeable element) comes from Compose/app code with theme-supplied colors, not from theme-authored animation. This is a deliberate simplicity/battery tradeoff and stands in direct contrast to commercial theme keyboards that sell animated themes as a premium tier. [uncertain: maintainer's current stated position on ever supporting animated backgrounds — issue comments were not retrievable]
